newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel venture capital funds raising record sums.
newsitem.headline: Israel venture capital funds raising record sums.

text.p: Israeli venture capital funds are raising record amounts of money but Wall Street may not be providing the same generous returns it has in recent years, speakers at a high tech investment conference said on Tuesday.

Yigal Erlich, president of Yozma Venture Capital Ltd, said Israeli venture capital funds had about $500 million currently under management but estimated the funds would raise another $800 million by 1998, virtually all of it for high tech.
Speakers said the surge of venture capital money was due to a buoyant U.S. market for technology issues that enabled Israeli companies to float at high valuations and give huge returns.

As recently as 1992, the government had felt the need to set up its own venture capital fund to encourage investors, said Shuki Gleitman, a former director-general of the Industry and Trade Ministry. Since then nearly 30 private sector funds had been formed and Yozma was privatised last month, he said.
"The industry of early-stage investing in Israel is about the same size as early-stage investing in all of Europe," said Jos Peters, who heads Belgium's Capricorn Ventures.

"The Israeli venture capital industry is only three or four years old, but we've been damn lucky," said Roni Hefetz, a manager of the Walden Israel Fund. "Wall Street was very strong in this period and we made a lot of money."

Matty Karp, who heads Kardan Technology Ventures, said 12 out of 17 Israeli initial public offerings (IPOs) last year were backed by venture capital funds. But he expected to see the market for high tech issues weaken by next year.
"I personally believe there'll be a downturn, which will have a direct impact on valuations for private capital."

Eral Margalit, of Oxton Israel Capital Ltd, said too many Israeli technology companies had gone public too early, which he and other speakers attributed to pressure from competing investment bankers and a bull market for technology IPOs.
"Many Israeli companies trading on Nasdaq don't have what it takes to be world class competitors," he said. "We've been holding companies back from doing IPOs."
Gil Shwed, CEO of CheckPoint Software Technology Ltd, attributed the problem to an absence of alternative markets for IPOs, which made firms turn to Nasdaq prematurely.

Shaul Bronfeld, managing director of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, which has been largely shunned by Israel's technology companies, conceded that companies should go public where they could fetch the highest valuations.
"In the last 20 years of Israel high tech industry, prices on Nasdaq remained better than those in Tel Aviv. It is an indisputable fact and we should not fight it," he said.

But he urged Israeli companies to pursue dual listings and said the exchange was working to make listings easier for technology companies. He said it had eased restrictions on selling securities after an IPO and would soon forgo its requirement for equity prior to listing.
